Works Progress Administration, “Model of San Francisco,” San Francisco City Planning Commission, 1940.

Source: [David Rumsey Map Collection](https://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/s/8d407x)

The [San Francisco model](https://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~313399~90082563:Composite--San-Francisco-Model?sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No&qvq=w4s:/where%2FSan%2BFrancisco%2B\(Calif.\)%2Fwhen%2F1940;q:san%20francisco;sort:Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No;lc:RUMSEY~8~1&mi=2&trs=166) was built by the Works Progress Administration (WPA), a New Deal agency, in the late 1930s. The model is made from wood, and measures 42 by 38 feet. The scale is 1 inch to 100 feet. The map presented here is a composite photograph of the [158 discrete pieces](https://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/view/search/who/Federal+Works+Agency%2C+Work+Projects+Administration/when/1940?q=san+francisco&sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No) that comprise the entire model. Altogether the pieces contain about 6,000 removable city blocks. The model is based on Harrison Ryker’s aerial photographs, which were also commissioned by the WPA, and which appear as a composite basemap on Imagined San Francisco.

A close comparison between the model and the Ryker basemap shows that the model is mostly faithful to the aerial photographs, down to individual buildings. However, there are some discrepancies. These are largely explained by the fact that the model was intended to be used as a planning tool–it provided a way for planners to visualize the city and imagine its future. For example, the area bounded by [Geary Boulevard, Steiner, Ellis, and Pierce Streets](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/maps-and-plans/#) appears as open space dotted with modernist housing blocks on the model, while the [Ryker photographs](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/maps-and-plans/#) show that the area actually contained dozens of houses and apartment buildings, consistent with the density of the surrounding urban fabric. The model was not showing the city as it was, but as it was imagined by the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency. The [1956 Western Addition A-1 Urban Renewal Plan](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/maps-and-plans/#) (which appears under the Western Addition Urban Renewal map group) is almost identical to the model, suggesting that planners removed the original 1940 blocks and replaced them with blocks showing the new scheme. Similarly, the [large freeway ramps](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/maps-and-plans/#) that run from Market and Octavia Streets north to Golden Gate Avenue do not appear in the [Ryker photographs](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/maps-and-plans/#), but do first appear in the [1963 Downtown Design Plan](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/maps-and-plans/#), prefiguring the construction of the Central Freeway.

According to [David Rumsey](https://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~313399~90082563:Composite--San-Francisco-Model?sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No&qvq=w4s:/where%2FSan%2BFrancisco%2B\(Calif.\)%2Fwhen%2F1940;q:san%20francisco;sort:Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No;lc:RUMSEY~8~1&mi=2&trs=166), the model was “first displayed in sections in the Golden Gate International Exposition on Treasure Island in San Francisco Bay in 1939. In 1940-1942 it was displayed in San Francisco City Hall. . . . In 1968, the downtown portion of the model became a research and planning tool in the Environmental Simulation Laboratory in the College of Environmental Design at UC Berkeley. The model has not been on public view, in its entirety, since 1942.”
